newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Pennsylvania law adds obstacle in Conrail fight.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pennsylvania law adds obstacle in Conrail fight.

text.p: As groundwork began for the legal battle over Conrail Inc. Thursday, legal experts and takeover specialists said Pennsylvania's corporate law could be an obstacle to Norfolk Southern Corp.'s bid to snatch Conrail from its planned merger with CSX Corp..

They said the law, which allows a company's board to act in the interests of groups other than shareholders, may make it more difficult than in other recent takeover battles to force Conrail to sell to the highest bidder.

"It looks like there would be greater protection given to Conrail's decision to merge with CSX in Pennsylvania," said Eric Orts, a corporate law professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School.
"Pennsylvania has the strongest anti-takeover regime in the country," Orts said.
"The fact that it (Conrail) is a Pennsylvania company is of tremendous importance," said one takeover stock specialist, who asked not to be identified.

Another takeover stock trader said the growing awareness of the Pennsylvania law contributed to a drop in Conrail's stock, which fell $2 to $93.625 on the New York Stock Exchange after rising $11.125 on Wednesday when Norfolk Southern announced its $100-a-share cash bid.
"This Pennsylvania statute is scaring the hell out of people ... there is no clear path for Norfolk to win right now," the trader said.
Also on Thursday, U.S. District Court Judge Donald Van Artsdalen scheduled a hearing for Nov. 12 on Norfolk Southern's suit to block the merger between Conrail and CSX.
The suit alleges Conrail violated Pennsylvania law and U.S. securities regulations in its merger agreement with CSX and in anti-takeover measures adopted as part of the deal.
A Conrail spokesman said Thursday the Norfolk Southern suit was "entirely without merit."
Norfolk Southern on Wednesday offered $100 a share, or about $9 billion, for Conrail, topping the proposed friendly merger with CSX valued at $92.50 a share, or about $8.4 billion.

Many major corporations, since they are registered in Delaware, are governed by that state's corporate law, which courts have said require corporate boards to act in the best interests of shareholders if the company is sold.
In 1994, in a highly publicized case, the Delaware Supreme Court forced an auction of Paramount Communications Inc.

QVC Inc. had sued for the right to try to buy the giant entertainment company after Viacom Inc. agreed to a merger with Paramount. Ultimately, Viacom won the auction with a tender offer preferred by Paramount shareholders.

But the Pennsylvania "corporate constituency" law, updated in 1990, states that company boards can consider interests other than shareholders, such as creditors, employees, and local communities, Orts said.
In Conrail's case, this could allow the company to cite such factors as an agreement by CSX to keep the headquarters of the merged firm in Philadelphia, Orts said.

"Generally in Delaware, you are not supposed to consider those ... you should be running the company for the shareholders," he said. "In Pennsylvania, it looks like, there would be no duty to auction," he said.
Conrail is a Pennsylvania corporation governed by the state's corporate laws.
Also on Thursday, banking sources said J.P. Morgan & Co. Inc. and Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc. have agreed to syndicate an $11.5 billion bank loan backing Norfolk Southern's bid.
Morgan and Merrill each would underwrite $2 billion, and they have provided a "highly confident" letter offering financing for the remainder, the sources said.
